text.p: Water filtration group Memtec Ltd said on Tuesday that it remained keen on acquisitions after being trumped last year in its US$280 million bid for medical filter firm Gelman Sciences Inc.

"I would confirm that we are evaluating alternatives as we speak. But nothing where we have any definitive agreements," said Denis Hanley, the founder and executive chairman of the high-technology company which has had most of its share market and sales success in the United States, where it has a NASDAQ listing.
Hanley said future acquisitions were not likely to be as large as the bid for Gelman, which was now owned by U.S.-rival Pall Corp.
"I would be hopeful that something would come to pass this calendar year," he added in a telephone interview with Reuters.

Describing Gelman as a rare opportunity, Hanley said Memtec was now focussed on takeovers which would add to the company's geographic spread. Currently, its operations were heavily weighted to the United States, which accounted for about half of total sales, followed in equal measure by Europe and the Asia/Pacific region which included the Australian headquarters.

Memtec acquired Germany's Seitz food and beverage filter company for US$52 million in the first half of calendar 1996, a purchase which has proved highly successful with Seitz emerging as the most profitable division in the 1996/97 second quarter ended December 31.

Asked if Memtec was looking for another big acquisition like Gelman, he said: "Not really. We are looking principally to expand geographically. I mean we have a lot of products that are already leading-edge and it is beneficial for us to be able to address a broader geographic market."

Hanley was coy when asked to reveal more about his takeover strategy, but indicated it was not likely to be in Asia, a region where the company wants to grow and has high hopes for the town water business in Japan.
"We have not made acquisitions in Asia, they are not readily available."

While acknowledging the recent problems at its Florida plant, which has also exercised the minds of a number of Wall Street analysts as they prepare their full year forecasts, Hanley said he was confident that Memtec would achieve higher earnings in 1996/97 (July/June).

The delay in expanding capacity at the Fluid Dynamics plant led to a sharp fall in that division's profits in the second quarter and has been responsible for the sharp fall in Memtec's share price this year.
The Australian Stock Exchange queried the company about the fall in its share price to A$28.20 last Thursday from A$37.05 just 10 days earlier. The stock reached a 1996 high of A$52.00.

"All I would say is that the range (by brokers) out there is indicative of reality. It might be down a little bit if there continues to be difficulties (at the Florida plant), or on the other hand it might be quite good," Hanley said.

Asked if Memtec could match the 1995/96 net income result of US$11.07 million, Hanley said: "It is possible, but a lot of last year's number was tax (benefits). We will certainly see a very significant operating income improvement, but I don't wish to speculate on a net figure."
